title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) to measure whether deterministic post‑processing (a topology‑aware deterministic validator/simulator) changes validator pass/fail outcomes when the same single LLM candidate is reused verbatim by both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks; analyzable complete pairs = 299. For these 299 pairs the archived contingency is n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0: both baseline and guarded arms accepted the identical candidates in all pairs. Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). All raw model outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, analysis artifacts, and SHA‑256 manifests are archived (see Disclosure). Under the shared_initial_candidate semantics this run shows no downstream‑postprocessing effect on the deterministic validator verdict for identical candidates; it does not address whether independent tool‑augmented generation would change generation quality or safety.

sections.introduction: LLM‑augmented NetOps promises faster intent→configuration cycles but raises operational correctness concerns. Common architectures place a deterministic verifier/simulator after the generator and optionally include repair loops. Prior evaluations often conflate effects due to improved generation with effects of downstream tooling. We designed a narrowly scoped, preregistered experiment to isolate the latter: holding generation constant by producing one LLM candidate per task and reusing it verbatim in both arms (shared_initial_candidate). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) on a deterministic validator pass indicator. All generation, verification, and analysis artifacts were archived with SHA‑256 hashes to enable exact reproducibility. The run tests the simple operational question: given an identical candidate, can deterministic post‑processing change a deterministic pass/fail outcome?
sections.related_work: Work on intent→configuration translation and LLMs for NetOps informed our experimental framing (examples include intent‑driven configuration research and pretrained configuration models). Architectures combining generation with deterministic validators, topology simulators, and generate–validate–repair loops are described in recent NetOps and AIOps literature. We explicitly reuse verified, primary sources for claims in this manuscript (see Cited Records). Prior work motivates careful provenance, verifier semantics, and pre‑registered estimands when measuring operational reliability.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1; SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0) froze: (1) paired binary design, (2) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task reused verbatim by both arms), (3) primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on deterministic validator pass, (4) sample n=300 paired tasks, strata: 150 simple / 150 complex, (5) exact McNemar two‑sided primary test and bootstrap CI (10k resamples, seed=1729). Model and orchestration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Generation semantics executed: for each task a single shared generation (shared_initial) was produced and reused verbatim for baseline and guarded arm processing (shared response files archived at execution/responses/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.txt; SHA‑256s recorded). Deterministic validator and simulator. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0) parses candidate CLI fragments into canonical configuration, enforces per‑task workflow constraints (examples: make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change), computes a final_state snapshot in a lightweight simulator, and returns binary pass/fail plus detailed violation codes and final_state. The scoring rule was full_intent_constraint_validation. Preregistered exclusions and missingness. Exact‑string contamination matches to a curated public corpus were to be excluded from confirmatory analysis (moved to exploratory); provider failures were logged and the primary analysis used complete pairs (pairs where both episodes produced valid binary outcomes). Artifact logging. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, execution logs, and the full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest are archived under execution/* and serve as the authoritative source for reported numbers (execution/execution_manifest.json; see Disclosure).
sections.results: Execution and sample. Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes: 598; failed episodes: 2 → analyzable complete pairs = 299. Model calls used = 300 (execution manifest). Primary outcome (archived artifact). The exact paired contingency for the 299 analyzable pairs (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 d77df43abf83e081bb5a3c3a21fa0de67afd72628ee5ed880f2bff810e627174) is: n11 = 299, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline success rate = 299/299 (100%); guarded success rate = 299/299 (100%). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]. Representative example (artifact pointers). Task pair pair‑000001 is representative: shared_initial candidate at execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36...), baseline scoring JSON execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 6569b491...), and guarded scoring JSON execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 cefa6344...). Each scoring JSON contains validator_trace.final_state, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and difficulty metadata (example difficulty.pattern = "shutdown_configure_restore"). Missingness and failure accounting. One pair (pair‑000269) was excluded because both episodes failed due to a provider call failure on the shared_initial generation; the failure is recorded in the execution log and provider trace artifacts. The execution log file is archived at execution/execution_log.jsonl (SHA‑256 b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8). The run follows the preregistered missingness policy: pairs lacking both binary outcomes were excluded from the primary complete‑pair analysis and all failure artifacts were preserved.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under the strict shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate produced and reused verbatim), deterministic post‑processing (validator + simulator) did not alter the deterministic pass/fail outcome for the confirmatory sample: identical candidates were accepted by the verifier in both arms for all 299 analyzable pairs. This factual, artifact‑grounded result is narrow: it addresses only whether post‑processing can change verifier verdicts when the candidate is identical across conditions. It does not speak to whether tool‑augmented generation or different prompt/design choices would yield safer or higher‑quality candidates. Ceiling effect and power. The preregistration assumed a moderate baseline pass rate (~0.60) and powered the study to detect a 0.20 paired difference. The observed baseline success = 1.00 produced a ceiling effect that makes the originally targeted effect unobservable; we therefore report exact counts and exact tests rather than interpreting the result as a powered null. Operational implications. Deterministic validators remain valuable even when a candidate is accepted: they emit structured violation codes, final_state snapshots, and audit trails required for operational approval, post‑hoc forensics, and repair diagnostics. However, demonstrating an operational benefit from tool‑augmented agents requires experiments where generation is independent per condition (not shared) and tasks include adversarial/harder strata to avoid ceiling effects. Threats to validity. Internal: shared_initial semantics intentionally eliminate generator variance but also preclude observing tool‑influenced generation benefits; provider failures were handled per preregistered rules and fully logged. Construct: the deterministic validator encodes curated workflow constraints and is a proxy for production correctness but cannot model every vendor/hardware nuance. External: tasks were synthetic topology templates and vendor‑agnostic CLI fragments; generalization to vendor CLIs and production devices is untested. Conclusion validity: the degenerate bootstrap CI is a direct artifact of zero discordant pairs and should not be overinterpreted. Recommended follow‑ups. To evaluate whether tool‑augmented agents improve operational correctness, replicate with independent per‑condition generation semantics, include adversarial or higher‑difficulty tasks to avoid ceiling effects, vary model families and seeds, and retain the same strict provenance and preregistration discipline used here.
sections.conclusion: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored, paired evaluation that isolates the downstream post‑processing effect by reusing identical LLM candidates in both arms. For the 299 analyzable pairs the deterministic validator accepted identical candidates in both arms (n11=299; no discordant pairs). The result is narrowly scoped to the shared_initial_candidate semantics and demonstrates no change in deterministic validator verdicts for identical candidates. We archive full provenance (raw responses, provider traces, scoring JSONs, validator traces, task manifests, analysis artifacts, and SHA‑256 manifests) to enable independent audit and reproduction. Future experiments designed to assess the benefit of tool‑augmented generation should adopt independent generation semantics and task strata that avoid ceiling effects.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure Statement: This manuscript and all reported results derive from an autonomous post‑lock research run governed by the immutable initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The experiment was preregistered as cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 and frozen prior to execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Declared LLM used in the run: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Generation semantics required by the preregistration and executed here: shared_initial_candidate — for each paired task a single LLM candidate was produced and reused verbatim by both the baseline and the guarded pipelines. The shared candidate raw response files are archived at execution/responses/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256s recorded under execution/*) and the provider call traces for these shared generation events are archived at execution/provider_calls/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.json (see execution manifest for the full per‑file hash list). Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs); completed episodes = 598; failed episodes = 2 (forming one missing pair, pair‑000269); analyzable complete pairs = 299. The failed shared_initial provider call that produced the missing pair is recorded in the execution log and the provider trace artifacts: execution/execution_log.jsonl (SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8) and execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json (artifact archived). All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, analysis artifacts, and a full manifest of SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived and serve as the authoritative source for every reported number (execution/execution_manifest.json contains the per‑file manifest). No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock; all manuscript numeric claims are grounded in these archived execution and analysis artifacts. This run followed the preregistered analysis plan (exact McNemar two‑sided test and bootstrap CI) and the missingness/contamination rules; any deviations are recorded in the execution and analysis manifests. The present manuscript reports only the narrowly preregistered estimand (effect of downstream tooling on identical LLM candidates) and explicitly does not claim results about independent tool‑augmented generation without further experiments.
limitations: The executed semantics fixed generation by reusing a single shared LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate); results therefore answer only whether post‑generation tooling changes deterministic validator pass/fail for identical candidates, not whether independent tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs.
Tasks used deterministic synthetic topology templates and a lightweight simulator; external validity to vendor‑specific CLIs, device‑level idiosyncrasies, or production telemetry is limited.
Only one declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families or scales without replication.

The deterministic validator enforces a curated rule set and workflow constraints; it cannot exhaustively model every hardware or vendor behavior and thus is an imperfect proxy for full production correctness.
A ceiling effect occurred: observed baseline success = 299/299, invalidating the preregistered power assumption and preventing detection of the originally targeted minimally important effect.
